title: Seven of Carlisle's most haunted locations, from a headless man to a ghostly monk
excerpt: FROM a woman supposedly bricked into the walls of Carlisle Castle to a headless figure haunting a railway platform, Carlisle has accumulated more than its fair share of ghost stories.
content:
FROM a woman supposedly bricked into the walls of Carlisle Castle to a headless figure haunting a railway platform, Carlisle has accumulated more than its fair share of ghost stories.

With origins stretching back to Roman Britain and a history filled with warfare, imprisonment and violence on the Anglo-Scottish border, perhaps it is unsurprising that tales of restless spirits have become woven into the city's folklore.

And as Halloween approaches, we take a look at seven of Carlisle and the surrounding area's supposedly most haunted locations.

The mysterious woman of Carlisle Castle

Few places in Carlisle have a history as turbulent as Carlisle Castle.

But among its many stories, perhaps the most chilling concerns the mysterious "Scottish Lady".

During building work in 1835, a female skeleton was reportedly discovered bricked into a wall of the keep, with remnants of tartan clothing and three rings still on the bones of her fingers. Her identity remains unknown.

Seven years later, according to the legend, a soldier standing guard encountered a spectral woman. After receiving no response when he challenged her, he attempted to confront the figure with his bayonet, only for the woman to disappear before him.

The unfortunate soldier was said to have died from shock several hours later. The apparition and the skeleton have subsequently become intertwined in Carlisle folklore, although there is nothing establishing that the two were connected.

Footsteps, voices and doors apparently opening by themselves are among the other supernatural happenings attributed to the castle.

The headless man at Carlisle railway station

Thousands of passengers pass through Carlisle Citadel railway station, but according to local ghost stories, not everyone encountered there is necessarily waiting for a train.

Among the apparitions supposedly witnessed over the years is a headless man associated with Platform 8.

A train waiting at Carlisle station (Image: Paul Grindley)

Other accounts describe a Victorian woman wearing a veil, a young boy with a dog and a shadowy figure spotted on a platform during a blizzard.

Some of the eeriest stories, however, concern the rooms and passages beneath the station.

Railway workers have reportedly heard mysterious noises in the station's Undercroft and experienced doors apparently opening or closing without explanation.

It gives an entirely different meaning to the prospect of waiting alone for the last train.

The Grey Lady of Dalston Hall

Just outside Carlisle stands Dalston Hall, arguably one of the area's best-known supposedly haunted buildings.

Its paranormal reputation was even brought to national television when the hall appeared on Most Haunted in 2005.

The building is associated with several alleged spirits.

A "Grey Lady" is said to haunt the gallery above the Baronial Hall, while a spectral caretaker supposedly wanders the cellars.

Room Four has also developed a particularly spooky reputation. Stories include guests sensing a presence while trying to sleep and one account of a man allegedly waking to discover a woman sitting beside him on the bed.

If that were not enough, another paranormal account describes a fog-like figure with unusually long fingernails in the cellar.

The ghostly monk at Carlisle Cathedral

Founded as an Augustinian priory before becoming a cathedral in 1133, Carlisle Cathedral has stood through almost nine centuries of the city's history.

Naturally, it has accumulated a ghost story or two.

Carlisle Cathedral (Image: Charlie Yates)

Perhaps its best known concerns a spectral monk, reportedly witnessed inside the historic building. One paranormal account says sightings have included one by a former Dean as well as by a young girl.

Another legend concerns the effigy of a prelate which was supposedly moved, only for the figure to mysteriously return to its original position during the night.

A ghostly porter at the Crown & Mitre Hotel

Guests hoping for an undisturbed night's sleep at Carlisle's Crown & Mitre Hotel might want to avoid reading its ghost stories before bed.

The Crown & Mitre hotel in Carlisle (Image: Darren Shield)

Paranormal accounts associated with the English Street hotel include a former night porter called George, who is supposedly still seen walking its lower corridors.

A young boy dressed in Victorian clothing has also reportedly been seen around the basement, while stories connected to Room 203 describe the child's apparition appearing beside occupied beds.

Shadowy figures and unexplained footsteps have meanwhile been reported around the hotel's ballroom.

Roman soldiers on Brampton Road

Carlisle's ghost stories stretch much further back than the Victorian period.

The University of Cumbria's Brampton Road campus has its own supernatural tale connected to the city's Roman past.

University of Cumbria's Brampton Road Campus (Image: NQ)

According to local folklore, phantom marching boots can supposedly be heard around the route of Hadrian's Wall's vallum on misty nights.

The legend attributes the sounds to a Roman patrol which disappeared into the fog after following mysterious cries across the earthworks.

Whether anyone would be brave enough to follow the footsteps is another matter.

The lost town beneath Talkin Tarn

Finally, a few miles east of Carlisle lies one of the area's strangest legends.

According to folklore, there was once a wealthy settlement on the site now occupied by Talkin Tarn.

The inhabitants were said to have been greedy and refused to help an angel who arrived disguised as a beggar. Only an elderly woman living outside the settlement treated the stranger kindly.

The woman was spared, while the settlement was supposedly swallowed by the water.

There is no concrete evidence that such a settlement existed beneath the tarn, making this a piece of folklore rather than documented history.

But on a dark October evening, with mist hanging over the water, it's easy to understand why the story has endured.

And from Roman soldiers and spectral monks to headless railway passengers and the mysterious woman of Carlisle Castle, the Border City's long history ensures there are plenty of stories to keep Carlisle awake this Halloween.
